spans.assertion: the adjusted risk difference between dark- and light-skinned players is 0.18 percentage points (95% CI [-0.02, 0.36]; p=0.128)
the risk difference corresponds to an adjusted odds ratio of 1.15 (95% CI [0.96, 1.38])
the hypothesis that referees give more red cards to dark-skinned players is not supported by the data
the point estimate suggests a slight increase in red-card probability for darker players but this is not statistically distinguishable from chance and could reflect sampling variability
the point estimate of the adjusted risk difference is 0.1757 percentage points (0.001757 absolute)
the bootstrap 95% confidence interval for the risk difference is [-0.0157, 0.3596] percentage points
the two-sided p-value for the risk difference is 0.128
the predicted red-card probability is 1.37% if all players had dark skin versus 1.20% if all players had light skin
the 0.18pp absolute difference represents a 15% relative increase but the estimate is highly uncertain
the confidence interval extends from a small protective effect (-0.02pp) to a modest harmful effect (+0.36pp)
the point estimate of the adjusted odds ratio is 1.1521
the 95% confidence interval for the odds ratio is [0.9599, 1.3828]
the two-sided p-value for the odds ratio is 0.128
the log-odds coefficient is 0.1416 with cluster-robust SE of 0.0931
the odds of a red card are 15% higher for dark-skinned players, compatible with effects from a 4% decrease to a 38% increase
the odds-ratio confidence interval includes 1.0 (no effect), consistent with the primary analysis
the unit of analysis is the player-referee dyad, one observation per unique pair across all matches they encountered each other
the final analysis sample is 102,323 dyads
84,050 dyads (82.1%) are light-skinned
18,273 dyads (17.9%) are dark-skinned
the sample includes 1,255 unique players
the sample includes 2,797 unique referees
21,407 dyads (14.7% of the original dataset) were excluded for having no player photo / missing skin tone data
14,598 medium-skin-tone dyads were excluded from the primary analysis to create clear contrast groups
7,700 dyads were excluded due to missing position data
two independent raters coded player photos for skin tone on a 0-1 scale
the two raters' scores were averaged into one skin-tone value
inter-rater reliability was Pearson r=0.923 with 76.8% exact agreement
skin tone was dichotomized into light (0-0.25) versus dark (0.5-1.0), excluding the medium range
the dichotomization was chosen to create clear contrast groups matching the hypothesis and to avoid an ambiguous middle category
the outcome is a binary indicator of whether any red card was received in the dyad across all matches
1,017 light-skin dyads (1.21%) had red cards
239 dark-skin dyads (1.31%) had red cards
the unadjusted difference in red-card rate is 0.098 percentage points
log-transformed number of games was included as a covariate to account for exposure
position (12 categories) was included as a covariate to control for confounding by position
league country (4 categories) was included as a covariate to control for league-level differences
a logistic regression model was fitted: logit(P(red card)) = β0 + β1(darkSkin) + β2 log(games) + β3(position) + β4(league)
the primary estimand (marginal risk difference) was computed via g-computation / marginal standardization
standard errors were cluster-robust, clustered by player
confidence intervals were computed via percentile bootstrap with 200 iterations using player-level resampling
dyad-level analysis was used because red cards are dyad-specific
cluster-robust SEs were used because each player appears in ~79 dyads on average, violating independence
log(games) was used as a covariate rather than as an offset
an offset specification for games was rejected because the relationship may not be exactly proportional
position was treated as an essential confounder, citing Center Backs at 1.97% versus Attacking Midfielders at 0.71% red-card rate and that darker players are more likely to be forwards
league was treated as an important control due to compositional differences (Germany 0.86% vs France 1.65% red cards; skin tone distribution differs by league)
the overall conclusion is NOT SUPPORTED
the hypothesis that referees give more red cards to dark-skinned players is not supported by this analysis

the 95% CI [-0.02, 0.36]pp includes zero
the wide confidence interval reflects substantial uncertainty (imprecise estimate)

the 0.18pp risk difference, if real, would be a small but non-trivial increase (1.20% to 1.37%)
the data are equally compatible with no effect, a small protective effect, or a modest harmful effect up to 0.36pp
the odds ratio of 1.15 is modest and similarly imprecise (CI 0.96-1.38)

spans.note: caveat that multiple sensitivity/stratification analyses increase Type I error risk

spans.note: caveat that the observational design cannot rule out reverse causation or unmeasured confounding

spans.assertion: the study does not directly measure referee bias

a continuous skin-tone specification (per 1.0 unit increase) was analyzed
under the continuous specification, OR=1.29, p=0.024

spans.note: What This Analysis Does NOT Show subheading

spans.assertion: the analysis does not prove the absence of bias (cannot distinguish a small effect from no effect)
the analysis does not address individual referee behavior, only population-level association
the analysis does not assess other outcomes such as yellow cards, fouls called, or game decisions
the analysis does not establish a causal mechanism
even if the 0.18pp point estimate were accurate, over 100 referee encounters a dark-skinned player would be expected to receive ~0.2 additional red cards versus a light-skinned player
this magnitude is small but potentially meaningful at the population level

spans.note: seven forward-looking recommendations for future research (match-level analysis, foul-level data, video review, individual referee analysis, yellow cards, temporal analysis, replication) — these describe what future studies should do, not what this analysis did or found

spans.assertion: this analysis provides insufficient evidence to support the hypothesis that referees systematically give more red cards to dark-skinned players
the point estimate suggests a small positive association (0.18pp, OR=1.15) but is statistically indistinguishable from zero, imprecisely estimated, and sensitive to analytic choices
heterogeneity across leagues (strong in Germany, null/protective elsewhere) suggests any effect is context-dependent rather than universal
the significant continuous-specification trend warrants caution against dismissing bias entirely, but the totality of evidence does not meet the threshold for confirming the hypothesis
the favored, skeptical interpretation is that random variation, unmeasured confounding, and model sensitivity better explain the observed patterns than a consistent referee bias
the patterns in Germany and the positive direction of most estimates justify continued monitoring and investigation of potential racial bias in officiating
the final conclusion is NOT SUPPORTED, based on magnitude, uncertainty, and failure to achieve statistical significance in the primary specification
